title: AI agent governance in practice: How our accounting team tested an AI approver
summary: AI agent governance in practice: how Expensify's accounting team scoped, tested, and piloted an AI agent as the first approver on expense reports.
body_markdown:
Definition


**What is AI agent governance?** AI agent governance is the set of rules for where an AI agent may act, which decisions it owns, what stays with people, and how its actions are recorded and reviewed. You settle those rules before anyone writes the agent's instructions, and you revisit them each time the agent takes on more.


*TL;DR: Our accounting team made an AI agent the first approver on our expense reports, and we treated it as a change to a financial control instead of a feature we switched on. One narrow policy check, a test workspace, then one brave employee.*


Accounting wanted a policy check it could own and change itself, without waiting on an engineer. So the check moved into an AI agent that reviews every report before a human approver sees it.


Our internal accounting team has used and tested it, and the full rollout is still ahead. A lot of what's written about AI governance in finance is frameworks. This is what it looked like on one real control, with real expense reports.


## Key takeaways


- Governing agentic AI in finance means deciding where the agent may act and what stays with people, before writing its instructions.
- Deloitte: 77% of finance leaders are comfortable with agentic tools that act with some autonomy, but only 14% back full autonomy for critical decisions.
- In Expensify, the agent enforcing workspace agent rules can sit first in the approval chain, ahead of human approvers, and every rule change is logged.
- Test in stages, a test workspace, then one employee, then a whole workspace, and be clear about what each stage proves.
- Make accounting a co-owner of the change, not the recipient of an engineering rollout.


## What an AI agent governance framework includes


An AI agent governance framework covers five things, and every one of them came up in our pilot. Each answers a question you'd ask about any new approver, human or not.


-


**Permissions.** What the agent is allowed to do, and where. Ours approves or rejects expenses on reports in one workspace, only where it's the assigned approver, and routing changes stay with people.


-


**Human oversight.** Which decisions people still make. Human approvers still review reports after the agent, and only workspace admins can write or change its rules.


-


**Accountability.** Who owns the agent's decisions when one is wrong. For us, that's accounting, as co-owner of the control the agent runs.


-


**Monitoring.** How you see what the agent did and why. Its comments post to the report thread for everyone on the report, and every rule change is logged in the workspace's #admins room.


-


**Compliance.** How the agent fits the controls you already answer to. Ours touched SOX controls, so it was handled as a control change, timed away from close.


## Why we put an AI agent first in the approval chain


The policy check we replaced was custom code. Every time accounting wanted to change it, someone had to find an engineer, and engineers are busy people. I know because I hire them.


What we wanted was a workflow that accounting maintains directly. In Expensify, that's an agent rule, a plain-language instruction an admin writes in the workspace. It's the same idea behind[Concierge, our AI agent](https://use.expensify.com/blog/expensify-concierge-expense-tracking-ai-agent) : you describe what you want in plain language, and the agent does the work.


**As the first approver, the agent checks every report against the rules before the employee's manager sees it, so coding and documentation mistakes get caught at the start.** CJ Johnson, who’s part of our accounting department, explains why that matters to her team.


"RuleBot is set up as the first approver. As such, it is able to follow the rules and prompts that we set up and review reports before they go to an employee's approver. This reduces coding and documentation errors that go undetected until they reach the Accounting department, which removes manual corrections and follow-ups required by the Accounting department."


I'd thought of the agent mostly as a way to stop bad expenses. For accounting, the bigger win was fewer reports coming back to them for fixes.


See how Expensify checks every report against[expense rules](https://use.expensify.com/expense-rules)


## Define the control before you replace it


AI agent governance starts with a boring question: what exactly is the control? Ours was narrow. It stops cash expenses marked non-reimbursable from going through.


Everything else about approvals stayed where it was. Ordinary approval routing still belongs to the workspace, so the change touched one check and nothing around it, which made it much easier to test.


Timing turned out to matter more than I expected. The old check blocked a report from being submitted at all, while the agent reviews a report after it's submitted but before the human approver acts on it. **The policy is the same, but those are two different controls, and they test differently,** so write down which one you're building before you start.


If the rule behind your control only lives in someone's head, write it into your[expense policy](https://use.expensify.com/resource-center/guides/expense-policy) first.


## Give the agent a bounded job


The agent's instructions live as[agent rules](https://help.expensify.com/articles/new-expensify/ai-agents/Create-Agent-Rules) in the workspace. When an admin creates the first rule, Expensify adds RuleBot, the workspace agent that enforces them.


RuleBot only acts on reports where it's the assigned approver in that workspace. It sits first in the chain, and the human approvers stay right where they were, after it.


**A bounded job has three boundaries, and you can set them before you write a single instruction.**


-


**Where the agent may act.** Here, one workspace, as the first approver on submitted reports.


-


**What it decides.** Whether each expense meets the written policy, approving or rejecting it with a comment.


-


**What stays with people.** Every approval after the agent's, plus any change to routing or to the rules themselves.


Two details make this easier to govern. Every time an agent rule is added, updated, or deleted, Expensify posts a system message in the workspace's #admins room, so there's a record of who changed what. And the help center is upfront that agent rules are evaluated by an LLM and may occasionally behave unexpectedly, which is a good reason to keep a human approver after the agent.


## Test real decisions, not just the instructions


Accounting didn't stop at reading the agent's instructions. They built a separate test workspace and submitted reports they expected to be approved and reports they expected to be rejected.


When a result didn't match, they adjusted the instructions and ran it again. CJ's version is simpler: "Accounting needs to test the workflow to make sure that it is operating as designed." Trust, but verify. Then verify again in a test workspace.


The cases they tested:


-


**A cash expense marked non-reimbursable,** which should be rejected.


-


**A reimbursable expense over $50 with an explanation,** which should pass.


-


**A reimbursable expense over $50 without an explanation,** which should be rejected.


-


**A mixed report,** where the agent should reject only the problem expenses and let the rest continue.


-


**The comment on every decision,** checked to make sure it tells the employee what to fix.


Mixed reports work because an[AI agent approver](https://help.expensify.com/articles/new-expensify/ai-agents/AI-Agent-Capabilities) can reject individual expenses while compliant ones continue through approval, and its comments post to the report thread, where everyone on the report can see them.


## Treat it as a change to a financial control


Accounting flagged something early that I'd have gotten to later: changing who approves employee expenses touches our SOX controls and how they're tested. So we handled it as a control change, with accounting as a co-owner of the work.


That changed the schedule, too. The setup was timed around quarter-end and the AP close, and accounting gave the go-ahead before anyone changed the setup.


If your company isn't under SOX, the same questions still apply to whatever controls you have.


Who owns this check today? How do you know it works? What changes when an agent runs it?


Finance teams are right to be careful here. PwC's AI agent survey of 308 US executives, fielded in April 2025, found that[trust in AI agents dropped to 20% for financial transactions](https://www.pwc.com/us/en/tech-effect/ai-analytics/ai-agent-survey.html) , against 38% for data analysis. Handling the agent as a control change, with accounting involved from the start, is one way to address that.


## Pilot in stages, and know what each stage proves


We went in three steps, and each one answers a different question.


1.


**A test workspace.** This shows the instructions produce the right decisions on reports built to test them.


2.


**One real workspace, with a single employee.** This shows the agent works on real reports without getting them stuck or rejecting them wrongly.


3.


**Every employee in that workspace.** This is our next step.


A pilot of one sounds tiny, and it is. If something breaks, it breaks for one person instead of the whole company.


Neither of the first two stages proves the agent will catch every prohibited expense, so the human approvers stay in the chain after it.


How far you can take this depends on your plan.[Agents as approvers](https://help.expensify.com/articles/new-expensify/ai-agents/Create-and-Use-Custom-Agents) work on Collect, where a workspace has a single approver, and on Control, where an agent can sit anywhere an approver can be selected, including multi-step workflows.


## A checklist for governing an AI agent in finance


These six steps come from what accounting learned by putting an agent in front of our own approvals. They work for AI agents in finance whatever tool you use, including the[AI expense management](https://use.expensify.com/ai-expense-management) built into Expensify.


1.


**Start with one narrow control that already exists.** You know what it's supposed to catch, so you'll know when the agent gets it wrong.


2.


**Make accounting a co-owner.** The people who own the control should own the change.


3.


**Time the change away from close, and get accounting's go-ahead before setup.**


4.


**Test allowed, prohibited, and mixed cases, and read the comment each decision leaves.**


5.


**Keep human approvers, and widen exposure one stage at a time.**


6.


**Say what each stage proves, and what it doesn't.**


Finance leaders at larger companies are asking for the same thing. In Deloitte's[Finance Trends 2027](https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/about/press-room/deloitte-finance-trends-2027-finance-leaders-balance-ambition-with-accountability.html) survey of 1,434 finance leaders, 42% said their agentic AI ambitions exceed their current capabilities, and they pointed to the need for stronger controls before expanding adoption.


The rollout to the whole workspace is next, and I'll tell you how it goes. If you're putting an agent into your own approvals, I'd love to hear what you're learning.


— david


Founder and CEO, Expensify


## FAQs about AI agent governance


-


###


It's deciding three things before an AI agent goes live: where it may act, which decisions it owns, and what stays with people. For our approval agent, that meant one workspace, a yes or no on each expense against the written policy, and human approvers for everything after it.


-


###


In our case, an AI agent reviews expense reports against a written policy as the first approver. It approves reports that meet the rules, rejects individual expenses that don't, and leaves a comment on each decision so the employee knows what to fix.


-


###


Build a test workspace and submit reports you expect to pass and reports you expect to fail, including mixed reports. Adjust the agent's instructions until the results match, then pilot with a single employee on real reports before widening it.


-


###


Because it catches coding and documentation errors before they reach the manager or accounting. The human approver then reviews reports that already meet the written policy, and accounting spends less time on corrections and follow-ups.


-


###


Capture receipts as they happen, submit reports on a schedule, and let rules review them. In Expensify, SmartScan reads each receipt, reports can submit automatically on a set schedule, and an AI agent can review each one against your policy before a manager approves it.


-


###


Import your categories from your accounting system and write your travel policy as rules. Concierge, Expensify's AI agent, categorizes receipts, and an agent approver can check each report against the policy first, so managers mostly see expenses that already follow it.
